speaker: Ms Valerie Lee
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) what considerations led to the original decision to permit limited screenings of the film “Dear You” in its original Teochew version rather than subtitled wider screenings; and (b) what factors will guide the Ministry’s more flexible approach towards permitting future dialect film screenings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) whether the Ministry will review the Film Classification Guidelines to allow Chinese dialect films, including the film “Dear You,” to have a general commercial release with their original audio instead of restricting them to niche screenings; (b) why foreign language films face no equivalent linguistic audio restrictions; and (c) whether the historical rationale for mandatory Mandarin dubbing remains relevant to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) whether the Ministry will abolish the guideline that Chinese films for general release be in Mandarin and allow dialect films on general release in their original dialect with subtitles; and (b) whether the Speak Mandarin Campaign rationale for the guideline still applies, given that dialect use at home has fallen below 12%.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) whether the framework for classifying dialect language films for general release includes any assessment of Intangible Cultural Heritage value; and (b) if not, whether the Ministry will work with the National Heritage Board to incorporate such an assessment.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) what factors are taken into account in Infocomm Media Development Authority's (IMDA) decision for the film "Dear You" to be dubbed in Mandarin for general screening instead of the original Teochew version; (b) whether heritage and cultural preservation value formed part of the assessment; and (c) whether IMDA will consider giving greater weight to heritage and cultural preservation value in future assessments.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information whether the Ministry will consider reviewing its policy to liberalise or abolish its language requirements with respect to Chinese dialects for media such as films and theatre, since the bilingual policy has reduced the use of dialects to less than 0.8% of Chinese households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information (a) what is the percentage of households that primarily speak Chinese dialects at home today as compared to 1979 when the Speak Mandarin Campaign was launched; (b) whether the Government sees the need to review the relevance of the Chinese dialect policy in its current form; and (c) if so, what considerations will be taken into account in any such review.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Tan, you will be taking Question Nos 6 to 12?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If Members are satisfied with the response, they may wish to withdraw their questions after this session.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Guidelines on language use in media are implemented by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They support the Government's longstanding policy to promote Mandarin as one of four official languages and have generally served us well.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, as noted in the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth's (MCCY's) earlier reply today, Singapore's language environment has evolved.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Recognising this, in implementing the guidelines, IMDA has exercised greater flexibility to allow more dialect content in films.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Each year, around 30 to 40 dialect films are screened at film festivals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, IMDA has allowed unrestricted screenings of films with substantial use of dialect, such as "881", "Long Long Time Ago" and "Wonderland".

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In doing so, we should also take into account the different media platforms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, there are no dialect restrictions for arts performances or content available on the Internet and online streaming services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On free-to-air television and radio, we believe that Mandarin should continue to be the mainstay.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We appreciate the feedback from Members and will carefully consider what further steps are appropriate.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first question to the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) is, today, cinema is the only mainstream medium in Singapore where Chinese dialect content is restricted.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over-the-top (OTT) streaming on social media platforms and YouTube all already carry dialect content without equivalent restrictions.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should cinema remain subject to the campaign's dialect restriction rationale?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also a commercial case, our cinema operators have been under real pressure. "Dear You" shows that original dialect programming can be an asset, not a niche indulgence. "Dear You" has drawn families off their sofas and back into theatres, together across generations, including older Singaporeans, who, otherwise, might not step into a cinema at all.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry go further in the review to consider removing this default restriction?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, "The master leads you through the door, but the practice is yours to pursue." Yet dialect arts face a more fundamental problem today – the masters are growing old and no young people are walking through that door.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Dialect artists are gradually passing on, with no one to carry the torch, and the flame risks being extinguished.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What concrete plans does the MCCY have to support the preservation of dialect arts and ensure that they continue to thrive in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mandarin is the bridge that connects us in society.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Dialect is what connects us, heart to heart, with our grandparents at home.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I have explained in my reply, we are getting feedback from different parties – industry stakeholders and community partners.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We appreciate and welcome the conversations that have arisen from the "Dear You" screening.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Actually, just yesterday, I had a screening in my constituency for my residents – one theatre in Teochew, one theatre in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I went by, spoke to my residents before my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For the Teochew hall, almost all seniors, maybe some of the middle-aged people, like me, were there.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Some were there because they wanted to hear the original Teochew dialect, some had watched the Mandarin one and wanted to hear the Teochew one.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When I went to the Mandarin hall, it was very interesting.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Some had actually watched the Teochew one and wanted to watch the Mandarin one because they could not quite understand the Teochew dialect, especially for non-Teochew speaking or non-native-Teochew speaking individuals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But in addition to seniors, I was very pleasantly surprised to see many young people – children, secondary school, even primary school.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They were there, accompanying their grandparents, parents and it was very good to see that it was a family affair.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The young people, when I spoke to them, wanted to understand more about the environment in which their great-grandparents or grandparents had lived through in the early days of Independence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But more importantly, having a Mandarin version creates a bigger access to many more audiences in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Not just those who are speaking the dialect, especially our young people.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, there is value in having a Mandarin version of the film, in addition to being aligned with our broader language policy.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Member mentioned OTT platforms, Internet streaming for example.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Different platforms have, historically, been regulated differently based on different reach of audiences.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Cinemas, being a public-regulated exhibition space in Singapore, ought to be seen closer to mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have been updating it, refining it, adapting them – for example, providing more flexibility of dialect use in films and in some of the mainstream radio stations and television channels.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, our policy, whilst remaining true to the policy intent of the larger language policy in Singapore, the implementation of it has evolved, has been flexible, pragmatic, taking into consideration the language environment.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I mentioned earlier in my reply, some of the local movies, like "881", have substantive dialect content in the film.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We look at the historical context, the heritage value and if it reflects Singapore stories.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: IMDA has taken a flexible, pragmatic approach and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chinese dialect art forms are an important part of the traditional arts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Over the years, the National Arts Council (NAC) has nurtured and supported Chinese dialect art forms through funding arts groups and help them engage audiences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: For instance, NAC funds the Traditional Arts Centre (Singapore), which encourages the younger generation to engage with Chinese opera in different dialects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: NAC also invests in the next generation of dialect art form practitioners through scholarships.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: In addition, several productions of Chinese dialect art forms are on SG Culture Pass, connecting Singaporeans to our distinctive heritage and culture.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We will continue to expand the space for our Chinese dialect art forms and nurture the next generation of practitioners.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see quite a few hands, and we do have around 130 Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Just now, Mr Cai, I must say that the asking of your supplementary question was a bit too long.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You went a little bit into a mini-speech and I almost stopped you.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But it is a good negative example of what I hope not to see going forward.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am very heartened to hear Senior Minister of State Tan confirm that IMDA is indeed looking to expand space for dialects while upholding Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also very heartened to hear Minister Neo then respond to this by saying that dialects are no longer seen in competition with Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, they play a role in deepening cultural appreciation of our Chinese heritage.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask whether MCCY will be working with IMDA to review the relevance of the policy, which still requires permission for us to screen dialect films.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of trying to see where we can exercise more flexibility, why not consider offering the freedom of simply just screening these dialect films?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because if dialect is always the one that requires permission, then have we not already chosen a side?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have raised issues relating to the preservation and use of dialects in this House several times in the past, including requests to lift the broadcast ban.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, I am heartened to hear the Ministers speaking on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my view, the main competitor to Mandarin today is not dialect, but English.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And I say this, as I said before, we are reaching a tipping point with an ageing population, younger generation with limited exposure to dialects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And once this culture and heritage die off, there is no way of rebuilding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Government to really consider putting more effort to work with the clans and other civic groups to promote our dialect heritage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And a question for Senior Minister of State Tan.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do not think you have addressed my Parliamentary Question directly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: IMDA works very closely with different Government agencies including the NHB.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In fact, we work closely on films, the classification of films.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, there is no need for an explicit institution arrangement as they are already doing so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: More importantly, I think the Member's earlier point was whether we consider heritage, artistic merit and the context in which dialects are used in film.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And I would like to reply in the affirmative.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I explained earlier in my reply, and I gave some examples of some of the locally made firms like "881", "Long Long Time Ago" and many others.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We do consider the context in which the dialect is used in the film – whether it is appropriate, reflects the cultural context of the movie of that time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, "881" was telling the story about the getai culture and some of the nuances of it, the texture of it, requires dialect to be used.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I want to assure the Member that we do so.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have two supplementary questions, one for MCCY.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With fewer Singaporeans speaking dialects, the rich heritage tied to these dialects risk being lost.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What steps is MCCY taking to ensure that Chinese-dialect cultures are being systematically documented, preserved and transmitted, particularly to younger Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will the Ministry publish clearer guidelines incorporating the said flexibility for dialect general screenings and share them in advance, so that film distributors will know what criteria will apply to these films?

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: Chinese dialect cultures are an integral part of our distinctive Singapore Chinese culture.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: When it comes to documentation, the NHB works very closely with heritage practitioners, clan associations and all who are keen, and they fund them as well, to research and to document our dialects and cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: One example is the Singapore Amoy Association, which recently published a book on the essays about the Hokkien culture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: Another example is Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre's Culturepaedia.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: That is a repository on Singapore Chinese culture and it has documented specific expects of the Chinese dialect cultures, with articles ranging from languages, all the way to music.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: When it comes to transmission and education, we also safeguard and we expand the space for our dialect cultures through initiatives such as the Stewards of Intangible Cultural Heritage Award.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: I think the Member was with me last year at these awards.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: These awards are to recognise individuals and organisations who take on the strong role in promoting dialects within our context.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: I am also very glad to note that one of the winners of the youth award is Mr Adrian Ong, who practises and promotes Hokkien string and glove puppetry.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: We will continue to work with all our clan associations, heritage practitioners and all who are keen to document and to expand the space for our Singapore Chinese dialect culture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The focus of my supplementary question will be on the film classification guidelines, which currently state that, quote, "Chinese films meant for theatrical release should generally be in Mandarin, in line with the Speak Mandarin Campaign.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Films with dialect content are allowed on a case-by-case basis." For the past 40 years or so, has the Speak Mandarin Campaign not been geared more towards encouraging English-speaking Chinese Singaporeans to speak Mandarin, instead of changing the language speaking habits of dialect-speaking Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, why do the film classification guidelines still hold on to the past focus of this campaign by restricting the screenings of dialect films in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And be that as it may, can case-by-case basis in the guidelines be interpreted as allowing certain dialect films a general commercial release, without restrictions on the number of screenings?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As earlier articulated by the Minister for MCCY on the broader language policy, Mandarin is one of the four official languages in Singapore and is the mainstay.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The historical context of the Speak Mandarin Campaign is about promoting the use of Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At that point in time, the language environment was different.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And because it succeeded, that is why the language environment today is different.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our young people are proficient, competent with English and many with Mandarin as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The policy's objectives remain because they are important, as articulated by MCCY earlier.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But our implementation of the guidelines, of the regulations have evolved with the changing language environment.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today's conversation or debate here in Parliament around "Dear You" is a step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I have said earlier, we welcome views from stakeholders, industry members, community partners, people who are enthusiastic about the dialect culture, enthusiastic about on trying to understand the roots, their identity, including the younger ones.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will take some time to do so because it is an evolution, it is a thoughtful approach, speaking to people, making adjustments, not abrupt changes, like all good policies are.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I want to assure Mr Giam that for "Dear You", we have given flexibility.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we will take a review as it comes along and it is certainly something for which we will speak to all members, industry partners, community partners about, and take their views on board.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For my Parliamentary Questions that the Senior Minister of State answered earlier, I thank him for answering them because those are questions that my dialect-speaking seniors in Toa Payoh East and their families have raised to me.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first supplementary question is: as Singapore's population ages, does the Government regard original language Chinese dialect films as supporting active ageing, social inclusion and in particular, inter-generational bonding?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second supplementary question is: has IMDA assessed audience demand for original language Chinese dialect films, particularly among seniors and younger Singaporeans, and if not, will such an assessment inform any future policy review?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In Bedok, we have one of the oldest estates and many seniors, and of course, they hold dialect and engagement with dialect as a very core part of their identity, their life experiences.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I must add that beyond just films and cinema, there are many other venues for which seniors and those who are not so old, the younger ones, to engage with the dialect culture.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Clan associations, programmes, different streaming applications or even activities in the community.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, it is not just isolated or confined to films.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I mentioned earlier in my reply, when I visited the theatre that screened the Mandarin version of the "Dear You" show, there were actually more young people, more inter-generational engagements – because the grandchildren, the children came together with their parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And because it was in Mandarin, it was more accessible to younger people.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When we talk about inter-generational cohesion, engagement, it really goes beyond just language.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is about creating the shared experiences and a space which these conversations and dialogues happen.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, we will certainly consider the different inputs as part of the review.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But rest assured, to the Member, that there are many other options and venues for seniors or younger ones to get engaged with the dialect culture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Last month, I spoke with Teochew residents in my constituency and they asked me, (In Teochew): "Zuo-ni buay sai toi teochew hee?" (做呢唔使睇潮州戏?") Which means: why can we not watch Teochew movies?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, a simple one: which version did the Ministers themselves watch?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, I would like to ask the Minister to clarify the objective behind this rule.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government's goal to promote Mandarin, or to restrict dialects?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the goal is simply to promote Mandarin, will the Government review all measures that exist purely to restrict dialects, including those relating to film and broadcasting, and remove restrictions that are no longer necessary?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, dialect courses run by clan associations are currently open only to members of the respective dialect group.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government consider expanding eligibility to a wider audience?

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: (In Mandarin): First of all, we Ministers have no time to watch movies.   : But to the Member's question about the Hokkien and dialect classes, I think we work with the clan associations all the time and they are very interested in promoting their dialects, as well as all our own respective cultures, because like I said, they contribute very distinctively towards our Singapore Chinese culture.

speaker: Mr David Neo
text: And if there is a demand, I think they will be more than happy to extend their classes to more people.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: (In Mandarin):   Just now I spoke about measures regarding the screening of dialect films in my English speech.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This film has been deeply moving and has resonated with local audiences.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Teochew spoken by the characters has struck a chord with many people, especially our grandparents' generation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The film has also sparked broader conversations among Singaporeans about the restrictions on screening dialect films.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have listened to various views and are grateful for the feedback received.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to thank IMDA for its flexibility in allowing the filming of "Dear You" in the Teochew dialect, and for approving additional screenings to meet public demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The film's reception reflects a genuine desire among many Singaporeans to connect with their cultural heritage through dialect movies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am, therefore, very glad to hear that the Government intends to continue with this approach.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Earlier I spoke about the policy objective of the Speak Mandarin Campaign, and we have remained consistent and united on this objective over the years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The question is our measures – how might we show some flexibility when it comes to movie screenings?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In fact, we have always maintained a practical and flexible approach.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I mentioned in my replies to other Members, we have our own local productions such as "881", which contain substantial dialect content, and we have been able to adopt a flexible approach in allowing them to be screened. "Dear You" has generated a warm response among many of us.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to approach such films with a flexible attitude.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Thank you very much, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We have all been talking about movies, but I would like to take a moment to talk about radio stations.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As our society ages, seniors naturally want to listen to songs from a bygone era.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we can better look after our seniors by allowing them to enjoy their favourite songs in their leisure time.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I must confess, though, that I am not much of a listener myself.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: (In Mandarin):   What Members discussed earlier encompassed not just movies, but television and radio stations as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We feel that Mandarin should remain the mainstream language.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The primary purpose of the Speak Mandarin Campaign is, after all, to encourage the speaking of Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Over the past few decades, the entire linguistic landscape has changed significantly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When I was a child, it was very difficult for me to learn Mandarin, because the various Chinese dialects share certain similarities in pronunciation with Mandarin that can create confusion.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When I was at The Chinese High School, I had classmates who came from Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They had attended primary school there and later came to do secondary school in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They could write Chinese well, but when they tried to speak Mandarin, their pronunciation was not standard due to the influence of Cantonese.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On Channel 8, for instance, there is a designated morning slot for dialect broadcasts, particularly for the news.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We do want seniors to have avenues to stay informed about what is happening in the world around them, hence the flexibility.
